meta.title: Who really said "Be Nice to People on Your Way Up. You'll Meet Them On Your Way Down"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Jimmy Durante. The line was in print on 5 July 1932 crediting Hollywood wit Wilson Mizner; Durante only borrowed it for a 1933 movie.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Be Nice to People on Your Way Up. You'll Meet Them On Your Way Down'?
meta.ogDescription: Durante spoke a version in a 1933 film, but the saying was in print in July 1932 crediting Wilson Mizner. Even Walter Winchell credited Mizner.

answer.label: Not Jimmy Durante — actually Wilson Mizner
answer.authorDates: 1876–1933 · American playwright, raconteur and Hollywood screenwriter
answer.sourceLine: The line is Wilson Mizner’s. It was already in print on 5 July 1932, in a San Francisco Chronicle item that credits “Wilson Miznor” — a misspelling — advising a rising film star; Durante’s version comes in an MGM picture released in September 1933. Walter Winchell, who broadcast the saying that same week and is often given the credit himself, handed it back to Mizner in his own syndicated column two days later.

source.heading: The paper trail starts in San Francisco, not in a Durante routine

docMeta.dd: “Directs Traveler On Road to Fame,” San Francisco Chronicle, 5 July 1932, p. 9, col. 6
Profiles: Legend of a Sport — Part I
Alva Johnston, The New Yorker, 10 October 1942, p. 21 — later worked into his book The Legendary Mizners (1953)

source.excerpt: Wilson Miznor, globe-trotter, ex-Alaska mining chappie, scenario writer, playwright and sage of Hollywood, gave the following advice to a young and coming motion picture star: “Be kind to everyone on the way up; you’ll meet the same people on the way down.”
trail: 5 July 1932 — San Francisco Chronicle. The earliest known printing already names Mizner (as “Wilson Miznor”), giving career advice to a rising film star: “Be kind to everyone on the way up; you’ll meet the same people on the way down.” The citation was supplied to Quote Investigator by researcher Barry Popik in December 2014. Barry Popik ↗

7–9 July 1932 — Walter Winchell. Winchell used the adage on air on 7 July; the Pittsburgh Press quoted it the next day in a radio round-up without attribution. In his own syndicated column on 9 July he named his source: “Which reminded a wag of Wilson Mizner’s classic advice.” Quote Investigator ↗

4 September 1933 — where Durante enters. Brooklyn Daily Eagle columnist Art Arthur, in “Reverting to Type,” described Durante’s scene in MGM’s Broadway to Hollywood and flagged it: Durante “uses two lines lifted from Winchell’s columns.” Quote Investigator reproduces the item; the Wikipedia entry supports only the film’s release date. Quote Investigator ↗ Released 15 September 1933: Wikipedia ↗

10 October 1942 — The New Yorker. Alva Johnston’s profile “Legend of a Sport” listed the saying among Mizner’s philosophical maxims in the wording that stuck. Johnston (1888–1950), a Pulitzer-winning reporter, later built the series into The Legendary Mizners. Wikipedia: Alva Johnston ↗
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest known printing, and the surname is misspelled — “Miznor” for Mizner. Note that it is not the familiar wording: the version everyone quotes today descends from Alva Johnston’s 1942 New Yorker profile, “Be nice to people on your way up because you’ll meet ’em on your way down.” The smoothed “meet them on your way down” form appears in no period source we could locate.

The earliest is a San Francisco Chronicle item of 5 July 1932 and the familiar wording comes from Alva Johnston’s New Yorker profile of 10 October 1942 — both published well after 1930, so we treat the text as in-copyright rather than public domain and quote only the short passages needed to document the attribution.

author.name: Wilson Mizner
author.kicker: The man who actually said it
author.heading: Wilson Mizner, the wit everybody quoted and nobody credited
author.metaLine: 1876–1933 · American playwright, raconteur and Hollywood screenwriter
author.bio: Wilson Mizner (19 May 1876 – 3 April 1933) was an American playwright, raconteur and entrepreneur who is remembered far less for anything he wrote than for what he said. After stints as a Klondike gold-rush chancer and a Broadway playwright, he landed in Hollywood writing screenplays for early talkies — his best-known credit is 20,000 Years in Sing Sing — and helping run the Brown Derby restaurants with backing from Jack L. Warner and Gloria Swanson. He called those Hollywood years a trip through a sewer in a glass-bottomed boat, and his one-liners circulated so widely under other people’s names that his brother Addison complained he was being robbed of credit — a complaint this quote proves was at least half right.

You’ll Meet Them On Your Way Down,” rev. December 21, 2014, last updated September 30, 2024.

copyAttribution: Be nice to people on your way up because you'll meet 'em on your way down. — Wilson Mizner, as printed in Alva Johnston's New Yorker profile "Legend of a Sport," 10 October 1942. Commonly misattributed to Jimmy Durante, who spoke a version in the 1933 MGM film "Broadway to Hollywood"; the saying was already in print on 5 July 1932 crediting Mizner. Via quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a quote with three claimants and one owner. Mizner said it, Winchell broadcast it, Durante performed it, and a film star tried to keep it — and the two people who did the least to earn it are the two whose names it still travels under.

items.why: Durante did say a version of it. In MGM’s Broadway to Hollywood (released 15 September 1933) he tells a swell-headed movie star, “Never snub people on your way up… because you meet the same people on your way down.” But the Brooklyn Daily Eagle columnist who noticed the moment on 4 September 1933 wrote that Durante “uses two lines lifted from Winchell’s columns.” The credit hardened when quotation anthologies printed it in Durante’s stage dialect from 1952 onward. Wikiquote files it on his page under Misattributed. Wikiquote ↗

Winchell used the adage on his radio programme on 7 July 1932, and Reader’s Digest (June 1933) and The Golden Book Magazine (August 1933) both printed it over his name. He never claimed it: in his syndicated column of 9 July 1932 he introduced it as “Wilson Mizner’s classic advice.” Quote Investigator ↗

A 1935 column in The Bee of Danville, Virginia grumbled that the film star had given one of Mizner’s gems as his own in a movie-magazine interview: “Be pleasant to the people you meet on the way up. They are the same people you are going to meet on the way down.” Quote Investigator ↗

No period source reproduces the internet’s tidy “you’ll meet them on your way down.” The 1932 printing says “Be kind to everyone on the way up”; the 1942 New Yorker version, the closest documented ancestor of the popular form, says “you’ll meet ’em on your way down.” Quote Investigator reproduces every dated wording from 1932 to 1952 and not one of them is the smoothed form. Wikiquote does carry it — but on the strength of a 1994 secondary source, Stuart B. McIver’s Dreamers, Schemers and Scalawags, rather than a period printing. Quote Investigator ↗ Wikiquote ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator, working from citations supplied by researcher Barry Popik in December 2014, concludes that Wilson Mizner was probably the originator: the earliest known citation names him, Winchell disclaimed authorship in his favour, and Durante’s use came a year after the saying was already circulating. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: A gag about Hollywood, told to Hollywood
lead: Mizner spent his last years inside the machine the line is about. He wrote screenplays for Warner Bros. and helped run the Brown Derby, where the town’s ascending and descending careers ate lunch at adjacent tables. The earliest printed version is not a general maxim at all — it is specific career advice, given by a “sage of Hollywood” to “a young and coming motion picture star.”

He did not live to watch it become a cliché. Mizner died on 3 April 1933, months before Broadway to Hollywood reached theatres that September with Durante delivering his own version of it to a swell-headed movie star — the scene that would eventually get Durante the credit.
detailsBody: 5 July 1932, San Francisco Chronicle: “Be kind to everyone on the way up; you’ll meet the same people on the way down.” Credited to “Wilson Miznor.”

9 July 1932, Walter Winchell’s column: “Always be pleasant to the people you meet on the way going up—for they are the same people you meet on the way down!” Explicitly called “Wilson Mizner’s classic advice.”

June 1933, Reader’s Digest: “It pays to be nice to the people you meet on the way up, for they are the same people you meet on the way down.” Credited to Winchell, not Mizner — the version that spread furthest fastest.

10 October 1942, The New Yorker: “Be nice to people on your way up because you’ll meet ’em on your way down.” The earliest known appearance of the wording modern quote sites recycle, and it is back under Mizner’s name.

1952 and 1958, quotation anthologies: “Be awful nice to ’em goin’ up, because you’re gonna meet ’em all comin’ down” — printed in Durante’s stage dialect and credited to him, in Franklin Pierce Adams’s FPA Book of Quotations and Herbert V. Prochnow’s The New Speaker’s Treasury of Wit and Wisdom. This is where the Durante attribution hardens.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes Wilson Mizner was probably the originator; the earliest known citation is the San Francisco Chronicle of 5 July 1932 (p. 9, col. 6) crediting "Wilson Miznor" with "Be kind to everyone on the way up; you'll meet the same people on the way down"; Winchell used it on radio 7 July 1932 and credited Mizner in his 9 July 1932 column; the Brooklyn Daily Eagle of 4 Sept 1933 said Durante's lines in Broadway to Hollywood were "lifted from Winchell's columns"; Alva Johnston's New Yorker profile "Legend of a Sport – Part I" (10 Oct 1942, p. 21) prints "Be nice to people on your way up because you'll meet 'em on your way down"; a 1935 Danville, Virginia column accused George Raft of passing off a version as his own; FPA's 1952 Book of Quotations credits Durante with "Be awful nice to 'em goin' up…"; Barry Popik supplied the antedating in December 2014; Reader's Digest (June 1933) and The Golden Book Magazine (Aug 1933) credited Winchell.
Barry Popik's entry on this saying credits Wilson Mizner as originator, notes Winchell always attributed it to Mizner, and includes the 5 July 1932 San Francisco Chronicle citation.

Wikiquote's Jimmy Durante page lists the saying and its variants under the section heading "Misattributed", with the note "Originally by Wilson Mizner" linking to Quote Investigator; variants cited include Prochnow's The New Speaker's Treasury of Wit and Wisdom (1958), p. 409 and A Quote for Every Day (2011), p. 41. Durante's dates are given as 10 February 1893 – 29 January 1980.

Wikiquote's Wilson Mizner page carries "Be nice to people on the way up because you'll meet them on the way down" in the sourced Epigrams subsection, referenced to Stuart B. McIver, Dreamers, Schemers and Scalawags (Pineapple Press, 1994) — not in a Disputed or Misattributed section.

Wilson Mizner was born 19 May 1876 and died 3 April 1933; he was an American playwright, raconteur and entrepreneur, noted for bons mots including this one; he wrote screenplays for early talkies (notably 20,000 Years in Sing Sing) and helped manage the Brown Derby restaurants with backing from Jack L. Warner and Gloria Swanson; he called Hollywood "a trip through a sewer in a glass-bottomed boat"; his older brother was the architect Addison Mizner.
Broadway to Hollywood is a 1933 Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer film directed by Willard Mack, released 15 September 1933, with Jimmy Durante in the cast as "Jimmy".

Alva Johnston (1888–1950) was an American journalist who wrote for the Sacramento Bee, The New York Times, the New York Herald Tribune, The Saturday Evening Post and The New Yorker, won a Pulitzer Prize for Reporting, and wrote The Legendary Mizners (Farrar, Straus and Young, 1953) based on his New Yorker writings.

The Internet Archive holds a borrowable (access-restricted) scan of Alva Johnston's The Legendary Mizners, published by Farrar, Straus & Giroux, with subject headings for the Mizner family, Addison Mizner (1872–1933) and Wilson Mizner (1876–1933).
